title: The Agentic Web and the Bazaar Era of AI - Ramesh Raskar, MIT Media Lab
talk_summary: The talk is mostly vision and standards advocacy, with a few concrete architectural mechanisms around discovery, message brokering, and simulation-based testing.

takeaways.technique: Message-box broker in front of agent runtimes
takeaways.what_they_do: Incoming messages do not go straight to an agent's runtime; a message box checks the sender, handles access, filters spam/bad requests, and holds messages until the agent is ready.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Messages do not go straight to the agent's runtime. They go to the message box first.

takeaways.what_they_do: Each agent publishes a signed 'agent facts' record stating what it does, what tools it may touch, who built it, and how to reach it; peers check facts before connecting.
takeaways.evidence_quote: a signed record that tells other agents who this agent is, what it can do, what it is allowed to touch

takeaways.technique: Discrete-event simulation of agent networks from YAML scenarios
takeaways.what_they_do: Nanda Town runs a discrete-event simulation where a short YAML file defines a scenario, injects agents and traffic, and replays runs step by step; tier one uses scripted agents, tier two swaps in real models.
Agent hosting platforms use a sleep-and-wake architecture so idle agents do not keep burning compute, addressing per-agent cost when running many agents.
takeaways.evidence_quote: sleep and wake architecture, so idle agents do not keep burning compute

takeaways.technique: Adaptive resolution / many endpoints per identity
takeaways.what_they_do: The index does not map one name to one fixed address; it returns updated facts based on who is asking and what they may access, so one agent can have many endpoints and traffic routes to the best one.
takeaways.evidence_quote: one agent can have many endpoints. Traffic can be routed to the best one
